Shawn Oliver suspends lieutenant governor campaign after OUI charge

“After careful reflection, I have made the decision to suspend my campaign for Lieutenant Governor,” Oliver said in a statement shared Sunday afternoon by a spokesperson for the state Republican Party. “This election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters. I want to sincerely thank everyone who has supported me throughout this journey and ask that my family’s privacy be respected during this difficult time.”With early voting already underway and hundreds of thousands of people already having submitted their ballots by mail, Oliver’s name will remain on voters’ ballots alongside Minogue’s. Minogue said earlier Sunday that beyond calling on Oliver to end his campaign, he would “formally ask for his resignation” should both he and the New Bedford city councilor be elected Nov. 3. Minogue and Oliver were challenging Governor Maura Healey and Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll, both first-term Democrats who have led the Republican nominees by a wide margin in public polling.A New Bedford police spokesperson said officers responded around 11:40 p.m. on Saturday to a crash on Dartmouth Street, where a vehicle, allegedly driven by Oliver, smashed into five vehicles, two of which sustained “extensive damage.”The crash scene on Dartmouth Street in New Bedford in the late evening on Saturday. The operator, City Councilor Shawn Oliver, was charged with operating under the influence of alcohol and released from jail the following morning.Courtesy of Joanne Doherty/The New Bedford LightOliver, 42, was transported to St. Luke’s Hospital to be treated for injuries from the crash, police said. He was arrested and charged with operating under the influence of liquor, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, a marked lanes violation, and speeding. Oliver was booked early Sunday morning in a New Bedford jail, according to the Bristol County sheriff’s office. Bristol County Sheriff Paul Heroux told the Globe that Oliver spent less than three hours in the Ash Street jail before he was released Sunday morning.Jennifer Sowa, a spokesperson for the Bristol district attorney’s office, said Oliver is expected to be arraigned Monday in New Bedford District Court. Neither Oliver nor a spokesperson for his campaign responded to requests for comment Sunday.Amy Carnevale, the chair of the state Republican Party, said in a statement Sunday that the party “supports” Oliver’s decision to suspend his campaign.“Lives were put at risk and that is never acceptable,” Carnevale said. Despite Oliver’s quick decision to step aside, the episode could complicate Republicans’ push to win the governor’s office and give Democrats a new line of attack in the crucial home stretch of the campaign. “It’s an unforced error,” said Republican state Senator Peter Durant. “What every campaign looks for is an October surprise, and unfortunately, that was just handed to Democrats on a silver platter.”Still, some within the party don’t expect the turbulence to throw Minogue’s campaign far off course. “I’m very disappointed, but you know, the election will go on, and I think we have a great candidate topping the ticket,” state Representative David DeCoste said. Despite the last-minute upheaval, the Norwell Republican said he doesn’t expect the development to significantly sway the outcome of the governor’s race. “The overall impact I think is going to be minimal because people weren’t making a judgment on how to vote based on the lieutenant governor candidates,” DeCoste said. While Oliver’s arrest and subsequent decision to press pause on his campaign is “a very unfortunate bump,” said Wendy Wakeman, a Republican strategist based in the state, it’s potentially a small one, given the role Oliver was running for technically carries few formal responsibilities. “You’re talking about the statewide position on the ballot that has the lowest stakes of all, right?” she said. Aside from serving as a stand-in for the governor should he or she become too sick to serve, die, or leave office, a lieutenant governor’s only other constitutional duty is to preside over the Governor’s Council, the eight-member body responsible for approving judicial nominees.GOP voters tapped Oliver as their nominee in September after an already tumultuous stretch for the Republican ticket. Anne Brensley, whom both Minogue and party activists endorsed in April for lieutenant governor, failed to qualify for the primary ballot amid a signature fraud scandal that shook the Republican ticket.GOP nominee Michael Minogue (right) spoke during his final gubernatorial debate Thursday against Governor Maura Healey.Danielle Parhizkaran/Globe StaffOliver then challenged the signatures submitted by one of his other one-time primary rivals, Anne Manning Martin, who was later knocked off the ballot after a judge said there was “substantial, if not overwhelming evidence” that her campaign submitted fraudulent voter signatures in order to qualify.The episode put Oliver and his then-running mate, Brian Shortsleeve, at odds with party leaders and Minogue, who called Oliver “shameful” and accused him of locking arms with “bad actors.”Minogue and Oliver ultimately became a team after both won their party nominations. But Oliver did not appear with Minogue at an event he held a week after the primary to lay out his campaign platform, and Minogue’s campaign materials have rarely mentioned Oliver as his running mate.In a debate earlier this month, Oliver described his and Minogue’s relationship as a “new friendship.”“We are crisscrossing the state. The message is clear,” Oliver said then. “We are united on the issues that matter most: affordability, accountability, opportunity, and keeping our communities safe.”Ultimately, it was “accountability” that Minogue said led him to quickly call for Oliver to end his campaign. “As governor, I will put the Commonwealth first. That starts with accountability, something Massachusetts has not seen from Maura Healey,” the Hamilton Republican said in his statement Sunday. While Minogue and Oliver were scarcely seen on the trail together, both candidates have been campaigning on similar issues. Minogue has pitched himself as a law-and-order candidate. In their second debate last week, Minogue repeatedly criticized Healey over the arrest of LaMar D. Cook, a former Healey aide who is facing state drug trafficking and gun charges and federal fraud charges. Minogue also lambasted the Democrat for a response she gave during the debate to a question about the “culture of misconduct” in the State Police after a man was charged with raping a woman he brought back to the State Police barracks on Martha’s Vineyard while staying there as a guest. “Do things happen? Sometimes things happen, but I can tell you, [State Police Colonel Geoffrey Noble] and I make sure that swift action is taken,” Healey said when asked about the incident during the debate.Minogue seized on the remark as evidence of what he described as a broader lack of accountability across her administration.“The governor just said, ‘Sometimes things happen.’ That is unacceptable. A woman was raped,” the Hamilton Republican said from the debate stage. “And when you have people that break the law or do things wrong, you are judged on your accountability.”Durant — who supported Shortsleeve, Oliver’s original running mate in the gubernatorial race — lauded Minogue’s move to quickly call for Oliver to step aside. “As Republicans, we often talk about holding people accountable, and we talk about holding ourselves accountable. Fact-checking Healey, Minogue in final MA governor debate


	In the final governor’s debate before Election Day, Republican businessman Mike Minogue and Democratic incumbent Gov. Maura Healey argued over whether Massachusetts needs new leadership to improve its affordability challenges or if the state is already on the right path.
PolitiFact’s partner WCVB-TV cohosted the debate with WBUR-FM and The Boston Globe. We also fact-checked the debate in real time. 
As he did in the first debate, Minogue, a former CEO of a medical device company, attacked Healey over the high cost of living in Massachusetts, including electricity, while the governor defended her record on tax cuts and housing policy. 
The candidates argued over Healey’s actions related to a former official in her administration who was fired after an arrest on cocaine trafficking and earlier this week charged with federal fraud in a food benefits program.
Here is a fact-check of their remarks. 
RELATED: Massachusetts governor’s race debate: Live fact-checks of Maura Healey and Mike Minogue
Energy
Minogue: Healey “stopped the natural gas pipelines coming in.”
This accurately describes her actions about a decade ago. Amid today’s high energy costs, Healey has reversed course. On Oct. 1, Healey asked the Trump administration to speed up the expansion of natural gas into Massachusetts.
Healey said during the debate she stopped natural gas pipelines from coming into the state when she was the state attorney general because the pipeline developer wanted “ratepayers and not the developer, not the company, to pay for it. I stood up for ratepayers and I went to court.” 
In 2015, Healey as attorney general authorized a study that found Massachusetts didn’t need new natural gas pipelines to maintain power grid reliability through 2030. Her office followed up in early 2016 by fighting pipeline developers in court to block a plan that could have required ratepayers to subsidize construction costs. A 2016 state Supreme Court ruling barred the funding mechanism, and developers shelved both multi-billion-dollar proposals.
Healey: “To lower energy bills, I filed legislation that would save us about $13 billion.”
That’s supported by an independent analysis commissioned by Healey’s administration, but critics say it’s an inflated estimate.
Healey filed the Energy, Affordability, Independence and Innovation Act in May 2025. 
The analysis Healey’s office released estimated the bill could save electric and gas customers $11.58 billion to $14.35 billion over 10 years. It says the projected savings would come from reducing certain energy bill charges and changing utility oversight.
The Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance, a conservative advocacy group, said the estimate was inflated because it did not reflect the bill’s costs for ratepayers, including expenses associated with utility programs and grid improvements. The Boston Globe also reported March 21 that Healey’s legislation would cut funding from Mass Save, the state’s energy efficiency program, and could reduce its long-term benefits. 
Lawmakers are reviewing Healey’s proposal.
Minogue: Massachusetts is “one of the most expensive places for electricity.”
That’s accurate.
Massachusetts ranked fourth for most expensive electricity as of July 2026, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s latest available data. Massachusetts residential electricity cost 30.49 cents per kilowatt hour, exceeded only by Hawaii (48 cents), California (33.61) and Maine (32.41).
Candidates spar about fired state worker who was arrested for trafficking cocaine, then charged with SNAP fraud
Minogue: “Someone can get 18 pounds of cocaine delivered, and you didn’t fire them. They got arrested, then they got severance, and now they’re on SNAP benefits that you didn’t even check on.”
Healey (following other remarks): “I fired LaMar Cook before he was even arraigned.”
Minogue: “He was arrested.”
Healey: “I fired him before he was even arraigned.”
Minogue: “After he was arrested.”
Minogue (following more remarks from Healey and crosstalk): “If someone is arrested, you didn’t fire them. They got arrested with 18 pounds of cocaine. In the real world, you’re automatically fired. Then you don’t get a severance package, and then you don’t get to get SNAP benefits.”
This needs context.
LaMar Cook, who was deputy director of Healey’s western Massachusetts office, was fired after Healey learned he was arrested Oct. 28, 2025, for trafficking cocaine after authorities seized about 17 pounds of the drug addressed to the state office building where Cook worked. 
He was arraigned Oct. 29, 2025.
Earlier this week, federal law enforcement arrested and charged Cook with one count of wire fraud and one count of SNAP fraud. A judge revoked Cook’s bail after the new federal charges.
Cook applied for SNAP benefits April 6 and falsely claimed he had less than $100 in his bank account and was living in a two-person household of himself and his child. 
Cook’s annual salary before he was fired was about $130,000. Authorities found he had a bank account with more than $8,800 and received thousands of dollars in additional deposits, including payments from his mother who had recently won $1 million in the lottery.
Cook failed to disclose that his fiancée and her mother lived with him at his Springfield residence and his fiancée earned annual income exceeding $80,000, prosecutors said.
Minogue’s description of a “severance package” was likely in reference to a vacation payout. The U.S. Attorney’s Office said the state paid Cook $22,374.29 in net pay for accrued vacation leave following his firing. Healey’s administration later realized an error in paying Cook for accrued vacation leave time and attempted to get it back but couldn’t, prosecutors said. 
Affordability and economic growth
Healey: “We have the fourth fastest growth — economic growth, GDP — in the country right now.” 
Healey: “In the last year, we created 15,000 jobs alone.”
Both statements are exaggerated.
The ranking for gross domestic product growth is lower than Healey said.
When measured by the average of the past four quarters of annualized GDP growth, Massachusetts is tied for 17th in the nation.
For jobs, the number is about half what Healey said. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show there were 8,300 more nonfarm jobs in Massachusetts in August 2026 than in August 2025.
Minogue: “In the last debate, Gov. Healey said ‘Massachusetts is a great place to live if you can afford it.’”
Minogue said several times that Healey had made this remark.
This needs context.
In an Oct. 8 debate, Healey was asked whether she supported a ballot measure that would encourage the construction of denser housing. She said yes.
“We need more homes,” Healey said. “Massachusetts is a great place to live if you can afford it, and that’s why I’ve been building homes from the get go.”
Minogue and his allies also posted on social media clipping this phrase, but excising the sentences before and after the quote. 
In tonight’s debate, Healey accused President Donald Trump of pursuing policies including tariffs that have increased the cost of building housing.
PolitiFact Chief Correspondent Louis Jacobson, Senior Correspondent Amy Sherman, Staff Writers Samantha Putterman, Loreben Tuquero and Cami Henry-Seymore and PolitiFact New York Reporter Conor Amendola contributed to this report.

Why is a pro-Mike Minogue super PAC targeting Mass. governor candidate Andrea James?


                                    Mike Minogue’s political prospects are looking bleak. This week, a UMass Amherst / WCVB poll showed Democratic Gov. Maura Healey leading Minogue, her Republican challenger, by 25 points, while a Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll put Healey’s lead at 23 points.With Election Day two weeks away and early voting already underway in earnest, you might expect Minogue and his supporters to be going scorched earth on Healey, attacking her on everything from outmigration driven by high housing costs to her oddly glib comment about an alleged rape at the State Police Barracks on Martha’s Vineyard.Instead, though, the super PAC backing Minogue, the Massachusetts First Independent Expenditure Political Action Committee, Inc., is running a video ad and sending out mailers attacking Andrea James, the independent candidate for governor who is running to Healey’s left. 
The ad, which is running on YouTube and premium streaming platforms, starts with an image of Healey. “Governor Healey is a do-nothing liberal,” the narrator says. “Her opponent Andrea James is a do-everything socialist. James is the Massachusetts [Zohran] Mamdani.”A photoshopped image of James and the progressive New York mayor smiling together near Boston Harbor then cuts to James herself outlining her priorities in a campaign video: “Housing for all, health care for all, child care for all.”According to images shared with GBH News, one side of the mailer also describes James as the “Massachusetts Mamdani” and urges voters to choose “common-sense Republican Mike Minogue” instead. The other side warns that while “Maura Healey is a liberal … Andrea James is a super liberal” who would, among other things, end all state cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and stop the construction of new state prisons.
    
    
        
        
        



        

        
        
        



        

        
    

    


According to federal law, super PACs are not allowed to coordinate with the campaigns they support. Massachusetts First’s decision to focus on James seems odd, given that she received just 6% support in the UMass Amherst / WCVB poll and a miniscule 2% in the Suffolk University / Boston Globe poll. But Rob Neuner, the chairman of Massachusetts First and CEO of the Connecticut-based canned oxygen maker Boost Oxygen, tells GBH News that the ad campaign is a matter of principle.“The big thing was … we thought, as [an independent] candidate, she should’ve been in the debates,” Neuner said of James. (James was not included in either of the two gubernatorial debates, which aired on WBZ-TV and WCVB-TV.)
“We looked into Andrea James a little bit more and figured she is someone that is showing the direction Massachusetts is going, and people should be aware of that,” Neuner added.
An attempt to lower Healey’s support?There’s another possible explanation — namely, that Massachusetts First is running ads decrying James as too left leaning in an attempt to convince some of Healey’s more progressive supporters to vote for James instead.This rationale was suggested in the analysis of an internal poll commissioned by Massachusetts First and released in September, which asserted that the “Independent, Progressive Candidate” in the race — i.e., James — ”Hurts Healey.”“Healey drops under the 50% mark on the ballot when voters are told independent progressive candidate Andrea James is on the general election ballot,” conservative pollster John McLaughlin wrote at the time. “While the little-known James currently pulls votes equally from both Healey and Minogue, it is a near certainty that she will draw more from Healey in November as voters become more familiar with her far-left politics.”Shortly after that poll was released, Minogue called on gubernatorial debate organizers to include James.Given the magnitude of Healey’s current lead, closing the gap in a meaningful way by luring her supporters into voting for James seems like a long shot. For the record, Neuner insists that’s not what’s happening.“Our polling showed otherwise, actually,” he said of the suggestion that Massachusetts First could prop up James to weaken Healey. “When James was part of the cohort that was polled, Mike actually got less [support].”This is also true. The same poll showed that, among voters who had seen, read or heard about both Minogue and Healey, Minogue led Healey 52% to 45%. When James was added to the mix, however, Minogue’s lead vanished and Healey led by 45% to Minogue’s 44%, with James pulling in 5%.There’s not necessarily a contradiction here, though. James may be capable of pulling from either Minogue or Healey, depending on how much voters know about who James is and what she stands for. A case could be made that this new ad campaign serves two complementary purposes: it makes it more likely that James will pull votes from Healey, and less likely that she’ll pull them from Minogue.But John Cluverius, a political scientist at UMass Lowell, contends that, at this stage of the race, it’s hard to imagine many voters vacillating between Minogue and James.“There are probably more progressive voters who are frustrated with Healey than there are swaying, undecided voters ... who are conservative who would back Minogue otherwise,” Cluverius said.The video ad and mailer, Cluverius said, “seem designed to elevate James as a spoiler to shave votes from Healey.”Jesse Rhodes, a political scientist at UMass Amherst, has a different take. He suggests that portraying James — who is the only Black candidate in the race — as a dangerous radical could be a cynical get-out-the-vote strategy.“A concern that I have, certainly, is that it could be a kind of dog-whistle politics, in which the [ads are] intended to elicit racialized anxiety by highlighting James’ positions … and trying to make voters who might be undecided or thinking about staying home anxious and mobilized on that basis,” Rhodes said.For her part, James says she welcomes the publicity.“Imagine the immense privilege it takes to think housing, healthcare, and childcare for all is a bad thing,” James told GBH News by text. “These attack ads are making my case for me. ... If making sure people can afford to live here makes me too liberal, I’ll be that.”

Healey, Minogue clash over costs, housing and energy in final Massachusetts gubernatorial debate

Healey, Minogue clash over costs, housing and energy in final Massachusetts gubernatorial debateWatch the debate againDigital Media ManagerNEEDHAM, Mass. —Gov. Maura Healey and Republican challenger Mike Minogue clashed Thursday over the cost of living, housing, energy bills, immigration and government accountability during their final debate before the Nov. 3 election.The incumbent and the former CEO argued over key issues as hundreds of thousands of voters across the Bay State have already received mail-in ballots, and others are preparing to make their decisions during early in-person voting that begins this weekend. Election Day is Nov. 3. Cost-of-living plansThe debate turned to issues of affordability several times, with Healey pointing to tax cuts and her housing initiatives while Minogue called for deeper reductions in gas and utility costs, according to their debate responses.Healey pointed to taxes she cut and said that she did not believe the suspension of the gas tax should be permanent. She argued that high prices are a direct result of the war with Iran and tried to link Minogue to President Donald Trump's policies."The first thing I did was cut taxes," she said. "I'm the first governor in 20 years to actually cut taxes."Minogue said he wanted to cut the gas tax, but also one-third of utility fees and a federal scholarship tax credit.Responding to official misconductMinogue criticized the governor's leadership and her response to incidents of misconduct, including the first arrest of former staffer Lamar Cook and the $495,000 settlement with a former MBTA employee who said Phillip Eng pulled her hair."It starts with the leader, and we've got to make sure that we have high expectations and we don't allow this," Minogue said. Healey pointed to her hiring of Col. Geoffrey Noble and the swift action that is taken when “sometimes things happen.""Do things happen? Sometimes things happen, but I can tell you he and I make sure that swift action is taken," Healey said. She thanked her law enforcement supporters and repeatedly said that she fired Cook before he was arraigned.Keeping energy costs down Minogue blamed high energy costs on Healey, arguing that she stopped a natural gas pipeline project while she was attorney general. He said that he would incorporate natural gas and nuclear energy into his energy strategy and argued that wind energy is too expensive to deserve a state investment."I am an engineer and I will invest in the innovation that is best for the future," he said. "That allows people to have low-cost energy, allows the hospitals to run 24/7, and allows us to do manufacturing."Healey responded that she asked the federal government to expand natural gas pipelines and said she opposed a previous pipeline because ratepayers would have had to fund the project. The governor said she is trying to lower energy bills by supporting wind and solar, and argued that those projects are easier to manage because they don't cross state borders. She said that costs are being driven up by the president's policies."I'm trying to get as much energy and all different kinds into Massachusetts as quickly as possible," Healey said. Federal immigration enforcementOn immigration enforcement, Healey pointed to the PROTECT Act and said she has stood up to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Trump.Minogue said ICE should coordinate with state and local authorities to target violent criminals and drug dealers. He argued that cooperation between the state and federal authorities is the best way to target people who pose public-safety threats. "Let's not have ICE going into the communities without coordination and without prioritization of the violent criminals and the drug dealers," Minogue said. Abortion policyMinogue did not directly answer whether he supports repealing the state's abortion law, instead saying he would follow the law and uphold his oath. He said he won’t politicize the issue. "I will obey the law," he said. "I will follow the law. I believe in the separation of church and state."Healey said it’s not politicizing something when 1 in 3 women in America don’t have access to abortion care. She talked about signing the state’s shield law and protecting women’s right to healthcare in Massachusetts.The two then argued over access to mifepristone. Minogue said the drug was Food and Drug Administration-approved, legal and available. He argued it was never going to be taken off the shelves. Healey said she stockpiled it because Trump had said he was going to take it off the shelves."I took that action because, at the time, Donald Trump said he was going to take mifepristone from the shelves, and I said, 'You know what, not on my watch,'" Healey said. Climate goalsShould Massachusetts roll back climate goals?Healey said the state should keep aspirational goals while focusing on bringing in new forms of energy, and specifically clean energy."We shouldn't roll back climate goals, but goals are goals," she said. "What matters is what are you doing today to operationalize something."Minogue pointed out that there are no businesses in Massachusetts that run on just wind or solar. He did not say whether or not the goals should be rolled back.Housing costsOn housing, Minogue called for universal "stretch codes" and faster state approval of projects.Healey highlighted a plan she said reduced permitting from one year to 30 days, expanded access to accessory dwelling units and provided tax credits to developers, according to the candidates.Flock camera backlashDozens of cities and towns across the state have paused or canceled their contracts with Flock Safety, a controversial company that provides automated license plate cameras for law enforcement. When asked about the issue, Minogue said the technology requires guidelines."I think we need guidelines, and I think people want privacy. I totally agree with that," he said.Healey said Flock is not used at a state level and said she is working on a framework to prevent future abuses of the technology. "Technology can be used for good. It can be abused, as it was by that police officer who was surveilling an ex-girlfriend," she said. Minogue then shifted the discussion to the Springfield courthouse project, criticizing the cost and contract. Healey defended that project. She said the existing courthouse had serious problems, that the project went through a procurement process and that a judge found the process "flawless."Racial wealth gapIn response to a question about how they plan to address racial inequities, Healey touted her first-time homebuyer program, action ending brokers' fees for renters, and making community college free. Minogue shifted the discussion toward education, arguing that poor educational outcomes contribute to the cycle of poverty."The first thing we have to do is give them the right education, give them vocational schools," he said. The one-hour debate was moderated by WCVB anchor and On The Record co-host Ed Harding. Panelists included WCVB political reporter and On The Record co-host Sharman Sacchetti, Boston Globe columnist Adrian Walker, and WBUR Morning Edition host Tiziana Dearing.In addition to consortium partners WCVB, WBUR and The Boston Globe, the debate was presented in collaboration with El Planeta and The Bay State Banner. DEDHAM, Mass. — With Election Day less than two weeks away, Republican candidate for Massachusetts governor Mike Minogue joined Boston 25 News on Wednesday night for a live, wide-ranging interview with Kerry Kavanaugh about his plans for the state and how he differs from Democratic Gov. He argued that state policies have contributed to the high cost of electricity, housing, health care and child care.Asked specifically how he would help public servants afford to live in the communities where they work, Minogue pointed to reducing taxes and energy costs as part of his approach.Trump and working across party linesMinogue was also pressed about his past support for Trump and whether the president’s standing in Massachusetts could hurt his campaign.Minogue said he had been an independent for 19 years before running for governor and stressed that he had previously worked with both Democrats and Republicans.He also outlined areas where he disagrees with Trump.“I don’t like the tariffs. I don’t like the NIH cuts,” Minogue said.Minogue said his responsibility as governor would be to work with whichever party controls Washington when it benefits Massachusetts and oppose federal policies he believes would hurt the state.“I will serve the people, not a political party,” he said.Immigration and ICEOn immigration, Minogue advocated for greater coordination between local, state, and federal authorities when federal immigration agents conduct enforcement operations in Massachusetts communities.“I don’t want federal agents going in unannounced,” Minogue said.He said immigration enforcement should prioritize people accused or convicted of violent crimes and drug dealing, while arguing that immigrants who follow the law should not be afraid to attend school or seek medical care.Minogue was also questioned about state policies limiting cooperation with federal immigration authorities. Michael Roger Minogue is an American businessman, military veteran, and politician who is the Republican Party nominee for Governor of Massachusetts in the 2026 Massachusetts gubernatorial election. A former chairman, president and chief executive officer of medical-device manufacturer Abiomed, Minogue entered the gubernatorial race in October 2025 and defeated businessman and former Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority executive Brian Shortsleeve in the September 2026 Republican primary.[1][2]

Before entering politics, Minogue spent nearly two decades leading Abiomed, a Massachusetts-based medical technology company best known for the Impella heart pump. He served as chief executive beginning in 2004 and remained at the company until its acquisition by Johnson & Johnson in 2022 in a transaction valued at approximately $16.6 billion.[3][4]

Michael Roger Minogue is an American businessman, military veteran, and politician who is the Republican Party nominee for Governor of Massachusetts in the 2026 Massachusetts gubernatorial election. A former chairman, president and chief executive officer of medical-device manufacturer Abiomed, Minogue entered the gubernatorial race in October 2025 and defeated businessman and former Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority executive Brian Shortsleeve in the September 2026 Republican primary.[1][2]
Before entering politics, Minogue spent nearly two decades leading Abiomed, a Massachusetts-based medical technology company best known for the Impella heart pump. He served as chief executive beginning in 2004 and remained at the company until its acquisition by Johnson & Johnson in 2022 in a transaction valued at approximately $16.6 billion.[3][4]
Early life and education[edit]
Michael Roger Minogue was born in Georgia and grew up in New Jersey, the son of an Air Force pilot.[5][6] His campaign has described him as the youngest of four children in an Irish Catholic family[7] and WBUR stated that he is a devout Irish Catholic.[6]
Minogue entered the United States Military Academy at West Point in 1985.[6] A company announcement shared after he joined Abiomed stated that he had graduate with a Bachelor of Science in engineering and afterwards earned an MBA from the University of Chicago.[3] Later filings described the West Point degree as an engineering management degree.[8][9]
After graduating from West Point, Minogue served on active duty in the United States Army for four years as an infantry officer.[8] He was a Ranger-qualified platoon leader during Operation Desert Storm in the Gulf War.[1][5] WBUR reported that he earned a Bronze Star Medal serving in Iraq in 1991.[6][10] A later Insulet filing stated that he was an Airborne Ranger.[9]
In 2016, Minogue told The Boston Globe that serving in infantry leadership meant "lead from the front," saying: "If you want to serve in these types of units, you have to serve something greater than yourself."[5]
After leaving active military service, Minogue began a career in the medical technology industry. He spent approximately twelve years with GE Medical Systems, holding a number of management positions in sales, marketing, cardiology, medical imaging, and information technology.[8]
Among his positions at GE were general manager of the company's global positron emission tomography business, general manager of Americas cardiology and information technology sales, and vice president and general manager for Americas sales and marketing for GE Medical Systems Information Technology.[8]
In April 2004, Minogue was appointed president and chief executive officer of Abiomed, a medical-device company headquartered in Danvers, Massachusetts. He also joined the company's board of directors.[3] He became chairman of the board in 2005.[8]
During Minogue's tenure, Abiomed increasingly shifted its focus from artificial-heart replacement technology toward technology intended to assist heart recovery. A major component of that transition was the company's acquisition and development of the Impella line of miniature heart pumps.[6]
Former Abiomed board member Dorothy Puhy told WBUR that Minogue presented the company's board with the plan to acquire the German company that controlled the intellectual property for the Impella heart pump, a transaction she described as beginning Abiomed's transformation into a much larger company.[6]
The company expanded significantly during Minogue's leadership, and the Impella became its principal product line. By the time Johnson & Johnson announced its acquisition of Abiomed in November 2022, the transaction valued the company at approximately $16.6 billion.[4]
Johnson & Johnson completed its acquisition of Abiomed in December 2022.[11] Minogue subsequently left the company.
Media reports estimated that Minogue personally received at least $153 million as a result of the transaction, with his total proceeds potentially substantially higher depending on his stock interests.[6]
During Minogue's tenure, Abiomed also faced regulatory and legal scrutiny involving some of its products and business practices. Federal regulators issued warnings and recalls involving the company's heart pumps, and Abiomed reached a federal settlement in 2018 concerning allegations involving physician payments and kickbacks.[12] Minogue has defended the company's record and has argued that criticism of Abiomed does not accurately represent its overall performance and impact.[12]
Minogue founded MedTechVets, a nonprofit organization intended to help military veterans transition into careers in the medical technology industry.[1]
He and his wife also established the Michael & Renee Minogue Foundation. According to his campaign, the foundation supports organizations involved in education, veterans' programs, healthcare innovation, faith-based initiatives, and programs serving children.[1]
Before becoming a candidate himself, Minogue was a significant donor to Republican candidates and organizations at the state and national levels.[1]
He supported former Massachusetts governor Charlie Baker and Republican U.S. Senate candidate John Deaton. Minogue also made substantial contributions to national Republican organizations and candidates, including the Republican National Committee.[1]
According to reporting by The Boston Globe, Minogue had previously changed his Massachusetts voter registration from Republican to unenrolled in 2007 before registering again as a Republican in April 2025. Voting records reviewed by the newspaper indicated that while unenrolled he participated exclusively in Republican primaries.[7]
Minogue and his wife also hosted or participated in fundraising activity associated with national Republican figures, including JD Vance. His support for President Donald Trump and other national Republicans became an issue raised by Democrats during his gubernatorial campaign.[1]
2026 Massachusetts gubernatorial campaign[edit]
On October 1, 2025, Minogue announced his candidacy for the Republican nomination for governor of Massachusetts in the 2026 Massachusetts gubernatorial election.[1]
He entered a Republican field that initially included former Massachusetts secretary of housing and economic development Mike Kennealy and former Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority chief administrator Brian Shortsleeve.[1]
Minogue described himself as a political outsider and made his experience managing Abiomed a central component of his campaign. He argued that Massachusetts government should operate with greater financial accountability and efficiency and said his private-sector management experience qualified him to reform state government.[6]
The campaign also emphasized affordability, public safety, economic competitiveness, housing, education, and government accountability.[6]
Minogue and Brian Shortsleeve were on the September 1st Republican gubernatorial primary. Minogue garnered 194,758 votes to Shortsleeve's 62,161, with 612 write-ins reported.[13][14] Shortsleeve endorsed Minogue on the night of the primary and said that Republicans ought to unite to defeat the democratic incumbent, Maura Healey.[15] Shortsleeve had previously argued during the primary that Minogue's opposition to abortion would be a hinderance in winning over moderate voters in the general election.[15]
On September 10, nine days after winning the primary, Minogue released a "Blueprint for a Better Future," which focused on affordability, opportunity, public safety, and accountability for the state government.[16][17] WBUR and The Boston Globe reported that the document calls for an outside audit of the state legislature and budget, a public spending dashboard, tax cuts, a gas-tax holiday when prices top $4 per gallon, the repealing of the state's net-zero emissions mandate, an end to sanctuary-state policies, and ending cashless bail. Maura Healey responded the same day by saying that "If he doesn't explain how he, as governor, would stand up to the damage that Donald Trump is doing to our residents, to our healthcare system, to our economy, that's not a blueprint."[16]
